games.title: Gun Fight
games.note: Two cowboys duel across the screen. Midway's US version of Taito's Western Gun was the first game to use a microprocessor.

games.title: Breakout
games.note: Bounce a ball to knock out a wall of bricks. Steve Wozniak built the prototype for Atari.

games.title: Space Invaders
games.note: Nishikado built custom hardware for it. The aliens speed up as you shoot them because fewer sprites let the hardware run faster.

games.title: Asteroids
games.note: Vector graphics and floaty, momentum-based ship controls. It became Atari's best-selling arcade game.

games.title: Galaxian
games.note: One of the first games with RGB color graphics, and the first to use tile-based hardware for multicolor sprites.

games.title: Galaga
games.note: Let a boss alien capture your ship with a tractor beam, then rescue it to fly two ships at once.

games.title: Defender
games.note: Often called the first side-scrolling shoot 'em up. A joystick plus five buttons made it famously hard to learn.

games.title: Scramble
games.note: A side-scrolling shooter where you bomb ground targets and watch your fuel, refilled by destroying fuel tanks.

games.title: Robotron: 2084
games.note: Two joysticks, one to move and one to shoot, against hundreds of robots while you rescue the last human family.

games.title: Xevious
games.note: One of the first games with a boss fight and a written backstory. It matched Space Invaders' sales in Japan.
A vertically scrolling Pacific War shooter where a loop-the-loop button lets you dodge enemy fire.

games.title: Gradius
games.note: Released as Nemesis outside Japan. Its NES version is where the Konami Code first appeared.

games.title: TwinBee
games.note: A cartoon 'cute 'em up' where you shoot floating bells to change their color and power-up.

games.title: Salamander
games.note: Released in North America as Life Force. It mixes side-scrolling and vertical stages.

games.title: Fantasy Zone
games.note: Its winged ship, Opa-Opa, served as a Sega mascot before Sonic.

games.title: Zanac
games.note: Its difficulty adjusts to how well you play, with enemies reacting to your skill and weapons.

games.title: R-Type
games.note: Its bosses and creatures borrow from H. R. Giger's biomechanical art and the film Aliens.

games.title: Katakis
games.note: So close to R-Type that rights holder Activision gave Factor 5 a choice: port R-Type officially, or be sued.

games.title: Parodius
games.note: A comic parody of Gradius where you can fly as an octopus or a penguin.

games.title: Thunder Force III
games.note: Lets you choose which of five planets to attack first, and switch weapons at any moment.

games.title: Raiden
games.note: Made after the studio's Dynamite Duke sold poorly, to recoup its costs. It spawned a long series.

games.title: Smash TV
games.note: A twin-stick arena shooter staged as 'the most violent game show of all time', set in 1999.

games.title: Xexex
games.note: Your ship carries Flint, a tentacled pod that can be fired off and recalled.

games.title: Project-X
games.note: A hard horizontal shooter from Team17, the studio that later made Worms.

games.title: Walker
games.note: You steer a giant war machine on legs and aim its guns with the mouse. Made by the later GTA studio.

games.title: Batsugun
games.note: Often called the first 'manic' bullet-hell shooter. Toaplan went bankrupt the following year.

games.title: RayForce
games.note: A lock-on laser hits enemies on a lower layer far below your ship. Also known as Layer Section and Galactic Attack.

games.title: DonPachi
games.note: The first game from Cave, co-founded by Batsugun programmer Tsuneki Ikeda.

games.title: Tyrian
games.note: A shareware shooter published by Epic MegaGames, with a shop between levels. It became freeware in 2004.

games.title: DoDonPachi
games.note: Fills the screen with slow, dense bullet patterns you weave through. Cave's second game.

games.title: Silhouette Mirage
games.note: A side-scrolling action game where attacks only hurt enemies of the opposite type: Silhouette or Mirage.

games.title: Radiant Silvergun
games.note: All seven weapons are available from the start and level up as you use them. Its Saturn copies became collector's items.

games.title: Ikaruga
games.note: Director Hiroshi Iuchi built the prototype in his spare time at home. Switch your ship's color to absorb matching bullets.

games.title: Touhou: Embodiment of Scarlet Devil
games.note: Made by one person, ZUN, who also wrote the music. It introduced spell cards: named boss bullet patterns.

games.title: Jets'n'Guns
games.note: A Czech horizontal shooter with a shop full of absurd weapons and a soundtrack by Swedish band Machinae Supremacy.

games.title: Geometry Wars: Retro Evolved
games.note: Began as a hidden arcade minigame in Project Gotham Racing 2. Once the most-downloaded Xbox Live Arcade game.

games.title: Super Stardust HD
games.note: A remake of Super Stardust, made for the Amiga by Bloodhouse, one of the studios that became Housemarque.

games.title: Resogun
games.note: A PlayStation 4 launch game whose voxel levels burst into thousands of cubes. It was free with PlayStation Plus.

games.title: Undertale
games.note: Made mostly by Toby Fox alone. Every fight can be won without killing, by dodging and talking.

games.title: Nex Machina
games.note: A twin-stick shooter made with Eugene Jarvis, creator of Defender and Robotron, as creative consultant.

games.title: Returnal
games.note: A third-person roguelite with bullet-hell patterns. Each death sends astronaut Selene back to her crash site.

links.took: Nishikado's earlier shooting game; it and electro-mechanical target games shaped Space Invaders.
links.added: Rows of descending aliens that shoot back, and bunkers that wear away.
links.extra: Gun Fight is Midway's US version of Nishikado's Western Gun.

links.took: Clearing targets one by one; Nishikado admired Breakout and wanted to make something better.
links.added: Targets that march, descend and shoot back, plus a high score to beat.
links.extra: Star Wars and Space Battleship Yamato gave it the space theme.

links.took: Shooting at an alien formation from the bottom of the screen; Namco wanted to rival it.
links.added: Full-color sprites and aliens that peel off from the formation to dive at you.

links.took: Galaxian's diving alien formations.
links.added: A tractor beam that captures your ship, which you can rescue to fire double.
links.extra: Galaga became more popular than the original.

links.took: Tile-and-sprite hardware ideas; Nintendo's Masayuki Uemura said Galaxian influenced Radar Scope and Donkey Kong.
links.added: Used colorful sprite hardware for a climbing, barrel-jumping platform game.
links.extra: Donkey Kong was built on Radar Scope's arcade board; Uemura said Galaxian also shaped the Famicom.

links.took: Space shooting; Eugene Jarvis's early prototypes drew on Space Invaders, whose launch drew him to arcades.
links.added: A scrolling world wider than the screen, a radar map, and humans to rescue.

links.took: Free-flying space combat from Asteroids, the other model for its early prototypes.
links.added: Side-scrolling with thrust and reverse, smart bombs, and hyperspace jumps.

links.took: Eugene Jarvis and Larry DeMar's own rescue-the-humans theme from Defender.
links.added: A single-screen arena with two joysticks: one to move, one to shoot.

links.took: Shooting robots inside a closed room, which Jarvis and DeMar drew on.
links.added: Hundreds of enemies at once, twin-joystick controls and humans to save.
links.extra: George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four supplied the setting.

links.took: Space Invaders' shooting, one of the influences Jarvis and DeMar named.
links.added: Enemies attacking from every side instead of marching down from above.

links.took: Eugene Jarvis's twin-stick arena shooting, with very similar play.
links.added: A televised death game show with prizes, a host and two-player co-op.
links.extra: Its themes were borrowed from dystopian films such as RoboCop and The Running Man.

links.took: The twin-stick control scheme Robotron popularized, which Geometry Wars revived.
links.added: Glowing neon shapes, huge particle explosions and online leaderboards.
links.extra: Geometry Wars began as a hidden minigame in Project Gotham Racing 2 (2003).

links.took: Twin-stick shooting in every direction, which Wikipedia says it combines with Asteroids.
links.added: Played on a small spherical planet, with weapons matched to rock types.

links.took: Big rocks that break into smaller rocks when shot.
links.added: Bosses, high-definition particle effects and a rotating planet to circle.
links.extra: It remakes Super Stardust, an Amiga game by Housemarque's predecessor Bloodhouse.

links.took: Housemarque's boost power-up and arcade scoring; Resogun is its spiritual successor.
links.added: A cylindrical voxel world that bursts into thousands of cubes.

links.took: Defender's scrolling world and rescuing humans, which Resogun draws on heavily.
links.added: A wraparound cylinder level, with survivors carried to escape pods.
links.extra: Wikipedia also names the Amiga shooter Datastorm as a source.

links.took: An enhanced version of Resogun's engine and voxel technology.
links.added: Top-down twin-stick arenas designed with Eugene Jarvis.

links.took: Robotron's creator: Eugene Jarvis served as creative consultant.
links.added: Rescuing humans under heavy fire, with a dash move and secret objectives.
links.extra: Polygon called it a spiritual successor to Smash TV and Robotron.

links.took: Waves, power-ups and score chasing from Jarvis's arena shooters.
links.added: Voxel explosions and global leaderboards for score runs.
links.extra: Housemarque's founders asked Jarvis to collaborate at the 2014 D.I.C.E. Awards.

links.took: Housemarque's arcade bullet patterns of spirals, rings and colored orbs.
links.added: A third-person roguelite on a shifting alien planet, where each death restarts the loop.

links.took: The side-scrolling shoot 'em up format that Defender began.
links.added: A charge beam and biomechanical enemies inspired by Aliens and H. R. Giger.

links.took: Horizontal shooting with power-ups; Irem's team drew inspiration from Gradius.
links.added: The Force: an indestructible pod you attach front or back, or launch at enemies.

links.took: Konami's own Scramble; Gradius began as 'Scramble 2' and reused its materials.
links.added: A power-up bar where you choose speed, missiles, lasers or Options.

links.took: A target to beat: the project's goal became surpassing Namco's Xevious.
links.added: Weapon choices that let players build up their own ship.

links.took: Shooting both air and ground targets; Namco wanted a shooter to rival Scramble.
links.added: Separate weapons for air and ground, a bombing sight and a backstory.

links.took: Xevious's vertical-scrolling template of air and ground targets.
links.added: Cartoon looks, two-player co-op and bells you juggle by shooting them.

links.took: Ideas from hit shooters; Seibu borrowed from Xevious, 1942 and Twin Cobra.
links.added: Modern fighter jets, a spreading Vulcan shot and thick enemy fire.

links.took: Vertical-scrolling air war against waves of planes, from Capcom's 1942.
links.added: A choice of spread shot or laser, and screen-clearing bombs.

links.took: Xevious's template of a vertical shooter with targets on two levels.
links.added: A lock-on laser that strikes enemies on lower layers far below.

links.took: ZUN made Touhou because RayForce had revived interest in shooters, which he loved.
links.added: A shrine-maiden heroine, Shinto themes and named bullet patterns called spell cards.
links.extra: The series began on the PC-98 in the late 1990s; this was the first Windows game.

links.took: Dodging bullet patterns; Toby Fox called Touhou the 'sole reason' for his games' battle systems.
links.added: Dodging inside a small box during turn-based fights you can win without killing.
links.extra: Fox spoke of the Touhou series in general.

links.took: Toaplan's dense bullet patterns; Cave co-founder Tsuneki Ikeda programmed on Batsugun.
links.added: Cave's first game, with a combo system that rewards chaining kills.

links.took: Cave's own bullet-hell shooting and combo scoring.
links.added: Denser bullet patterns, a revised combo system and a hidden second loop.

links.took: Treasure's own polarity idea, where attacks interact by type.
links.added: Black and white bullets you absorb by switching your ship to the same color.

links.took: Treasure's earlier shooter; Ikaruga began as a direct sequel codenamed 'Project RS-2'.
links.added: Chaining three kills of one color for points, on a single polarity button.

links.took: Gradius popularized orbiting helper pods; Thunder Force III's CLAWs copy your fire similarly.
links.added: Weapons you can switch between at any time, at high speed.

links.took: Gradius's ship, power-ups and Konami's horizontal shooting.
links.added: Alternating horizontal and vertical stages, with two players at once.

links.took: Gradius's power-up bar, stages and bosses, played for laughs.
links.added: Cartoon ships such as an octopus and a penguin.

links.took: R-Type's look, levels, power-ups and bosses, close enough to be called a clone.
links.added: Led to the official Amiga R-Type, which Activision hired Factor 5 to make instead of suing.

links.took: Designer Manfred Trenz, whose Turrican II hides a 'KATAKIS LIVES!!!' easter egg.
links.added: Run-and-gun platforming mixed with spaceship shooting stages.

links.took: A detachable helper pod and organic horizontal stages, heavily influenced by R-Type.
links.added: Flint, a tentacled pod that grabs at enemies, and lavish sprite effects.

links.took: Defender's side-scrolling format with a level that wraps around.
links.added: Pastel cartoon worlds and a shop where coins buy new weapons.

links.took: Compile's shooter style; Tyrian was made chiefly as a homage to Zanac.
links.added: A shop for weapons and ship parts between levels, and a story.

links.took: Buying weapons and upgrades between missions; Rake in Grass was heavily inspired by Tyrian 2000.
links.added: More weapons and gadgets, unlimited retries, and a metal soundtrack by Machinae Supremacy.

links.took: Team17's hard Amiga shooter, one of three games Rake in Grass named.
links.added: Dark humor and a shop of absurd weapons.

links.took: DMA Design's Walker, named among the games that heavily inspired it.
links.added: A side-scrolling plane shooter instead of Walker's stomping war robot.
